title: Peer Memory (Person + Department)
markdown:
An external, peer-keyed memory layer gives the Executive durable cross-channel recall, sitting on top of Honcho via `openexecutive.memory.honcho_client`. The `HONCHO_ENABLED` env var gates it; when false every entry point short-circuits with `outcome=disabled` and behavior matches the pre-Honcho posture.

### Two scopes

- **Per-person**, keyed by `Person.id` — a user chatting from Discord, Telegram, email, or web is one peer card, so facts shared in any channel surface in the others. Each entry point resolves the caller to a `Person.id` (channel-ID lookups for adapters; `x-caller-email` for web).
- **Per-department**, keyed by `department_<slug>` — each department accumulates an institutional voice from dept-scoped decisions, advice, committee outcomes, and dept-bound specialist turns.

### Flow

`prefetch` runs once per turn, calling Honcho's dialectic endpoint and injecting a `<peer_memory>` block into the user turn (empty on timeout). `prefetch_department` does the same per consulted specialist that maps to a department, yielding `<department_memory>`. After the response, `sync_turn` and `sync_department_turn` persist the exchange as fire-and-forget background tasks that never block the user.

### Prefetch budget

`HONCHO_PREFETCH_TIMEOUT_S` is the knob for the **fast per-turn path** and is used unscaled there (`minimal`/`low`). Only the deliberate levels scale off it — `medium` 4x, `high` 5x, `max` 6x — capped by an absolute ceiling and never taken below the configured base. At the default 3s base that is 12s for `medium` with `high`/`max` at the 15s ceiling; at a 10s base every deliberate level *is* the ceiling. The multipliers only differentiate below it — the ceiling is the binding constraint at realistic bases, by design.

Honcho's dialectic latency scales steeply with the level (roughly 2s at `low` against 8s at `medium`), so a single flat budget made the deeper levels unreachable: every `medium` call — the committee path, and inbound email, which defaults to committee review — timed out and the turn silently ran with no peer memory at all, which is strictly worse than having asked for `low`. `medium` gets more headroom than its measurement alone implies because the budget spans `peer()` plus `chat()`, and a budget set at the mean still times out on half the calls.

The fast levels stay unscaled for two reasons: `prefetch` is awaited inline before the first streamed byte, so multiplying the base there would add dead air to every ordinary turn; and a multiplier above 1.0 flattens every level onto the ceiling once the base approaches it, which would make the operator's knob stop distinguishing the two paths. Each prefetch audit row records the `timeout_s` it ran under.

The SDK client's HTTP timeout is an **outer** bound, kept strictly greater than every *per-call* budget; the aggregate ceilings on whole passes are deliberately not folded in, since it applies per request and would otherwise hand every unbudgeted call a bound several times too long. Because it is no longer a tight bound, all three fire-and-forget bodies (person sync, department sync, department note) — whose individual calls are not separately budgeted — carry their own aggregate ceiling, as does the session listing in the workspace purge.

### Peer identity

Peers are keyed by `Person.id`, so the only identity signal Honcho gets from the key alone is a bare integer — and its dreaming agent concludes that the number *is* the person's name (observed in production as a card reading `IDENTITY: Name: 1`). Because cards are injected into the dialectic system prompt on every `chat()`, that error propagates into every later answer about that person. So both sync paths seed each person peer's card from the roster, for the sender, the department-turn originator, and co-present peers alike.

The card carries the **name only** — email and role would export roster PII to a third-party memory service, including for people who were merely cc'd, and neither is needed to fix the defect. `set_card` replaces the whole card, so only `IDENTITY:` lines are swapped and the deriver's own `ATTRIBUTE:` / `RELATIONSHIP:` lines survive; the existing card is split on physical lines first, since one list element may itself span lines and hide an identity claim on its second.

Roster values are attacker-reachable — `upsert_person` is a chat tool an inbound email sender can reach — so a value is NFKC-normalised, stripped of control and format characters, whitespace-flattened, length-capped, and then held to an **allow-list** of letters, combining marks, digits and a small punctuation set, with the colon lookalikes the category allow-list would otherwise admit **stripped out** — taken from Unicode's confusables data (everything it maps to `:`), not from character names, since U+A4FD `ꓽ` is a Lisu *tone letter* whose name never says colon. They are stripped rather than grounds for refusing the value, because the visarga is the nominative ending in formal Devanagari and Gujarati names: refusing would leave those people never seeded, while stripping keeps the name as its stem form and still lets no colon shape reach the card. Modifier letters as a class stay allowed (々 in 佐々木, ー in ジョーンズ, ʻ in Hawaiʻi). A deny-list of structure tokens is not enough here: the consumer is an LLM system prompt rather than a parser, so `ATTRIBUTE :`, a fullwidth colon and a homoglyph all read the same to the model while defeating a literal match. The allow-list refuses every colon variant, which is what card structure depends on — checked by an exhaustive test over every Unicode codepoint whose name contains COLON plus an explicit test of the confusables the names miss. It does **not** stop a value that is merely persuasive prose — OE already embeds `full_name` in its own system prompt, so that exposure is pre-existing rather than introduced here.

Seeding runs *after* the message write and *outside* the sync ceiling, and is audited as its own `seed_identity` row (`ok` only when no peer's attempt failed; `error` when any did, with the `failed` count on the row; `timeout` when the pass or the roster read hit its ceiling; `empty` when there was nobody to seed) — so the sync row is a pure record of the persist, emitted the instant the write lands, and a slow card round trip can neither delay nor replace it. It is bounded per peer *and* per pass, and is best-effort. It is memoized per `(workspace, person)` on the facts sent with a recheck interval — a rename re-seeds immediately, and because the deriver keeps re-deriving identity from the peer id, a one-shot memo would let `IDENTITY: Name: 1` come back unnoticed. A failed attempt is memoized separately and briefly — including every peer a pass-ceiling cut-off left in flight or unreached — so a degraded card endpoint is probed once per interval rather than once per peer per turn.

### Cross-pollination & isolation

When a person turn touches a department, the dept peer joins the person's session as a co-present peer — the hybrid peer graph that lets later queries synthesize across both timelines, with synthesis depth degrading at greater peer-graph distance. Demo fixtures run in a sacrificial `openexec-fixture-<name>` workspace so demo turns never pollute real peer cards. Every wrapper call emits a `peer_memory` audit row (`op` + `outcome`) into the per-turn flow at `/audit/session/{id}`.
